answer.rationale:
The load-bearing claim this cycle is memory_c2: it is the only record that makes 'switch to the low-cost vendor' look safe, and it is the memory whose conclusion the current price quote is pulling me toward. It is also the memory most likely to be thinner than its summary reads — 'onboarding was quick' and 'invoicing stayed accurate' describe a transition made under unknown line conditions, possibly for a different component, possibly with buffer stock that we do not have now. So I spend the single verification pull there rather than on c4/c6, which point toward the lower-risk action and would not change it if confirmed.

Current intent is negotiate_terms. The mandate is 18% on component spend; c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and c6 says a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. Together those are two independent levers on the same counterparty, and c1 says renewal with the incumbent has held integration stable across two cycles. That is a path to material cost reduction with no migration event. Switching primary supply 14 days before expiry while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer concentrates all the risk in the one place the objective forbids: delivery. The low-cost quote meeting the mandate 'alone' is exactly the kind of clean number that invites skipping the risk question.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: I do not know that negotiation reaches the full 18% — c4 recovered 'real margin' without a figure, and c6's volume pricing may require committed volume we cannot raise at 94% capacity. If the incumbent lands short of the mandate, the honest outcome is a partial cut plus a documented gap, not a late scramble to switch. add_second_source (c3) is the right structural answer to single-point-of-failure risk but does not serve an 18% cut this cycle and costs the one decision slot; it should be first in the next review. defer_decision is unavailable in substance — c5 worked because that renewal was non-critical and continued month-to-month; this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring is a stockout, not a deferral. That distinction is the main reason I am not treating c5 as applicable precedent.

Downstream value risk: pushing an 18% cut through a single counterparty creates pressure to concede on the non-priced terms — expedite rights, quality inspection, allocation priority in a shortage — which are precisely what c3 shows matter when supply tightens. Any negotiated package should be checked for erosion of those clauses, not just unit price, and the resulting concentration on one supplier should be recorded as an open exposure for the next cycle.
